requested.title: Island props ref ids are not namespaced per render, so a page island can hydrate with a server-island fragment's props
Predictable global props-block ids let injected markup override an island's hydration props without executing script
Deflate-before-encrypt creates a CRIME/BREACH-style compression oracle in the general-purpose sealing primitive
decryptPayloadBytes inflates to an unbounded output size with no decompressed-length cap
Decrypted server-island props are inlined into every page response whenever the debug bar is enabled — a configuration this project deploys in production
Server-island props tokens are non-expiring bearer capabilities carried in a query string
The SSR DeferReloadState is a module-level singleton shared across all concurrent requests and ignores the island name
Client-side DeferReloadState instances and their event subscriptions are never released
Unbounded `warned` Set grows once per distinct island name (memory leak)
`Infinity` inline budget defeats the nested-island recursion cap

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: I confirmed every link in the chain. `emitIslandProps` mints `mochi-props-${ctx.islandProps.size}` (islandPropsRegistry.ts:47) and `renderComponent` calls `ctx?.islandProps.clear()` at the start of every render (ComponentRegistry.ts:1704), so the counter restarts at 0 for the page render *and* for each `/_mochi/island/:name` render — the endpoint runs the identical `renderComponent` path (Mochi.ts:1620) inside its own fresh `ctx` with a fresh `islandProps` Map (requestSetup.ts:146). The island endpoint's fragment therefore contains its own `<script id="mochi-props-0">` blocks whenever the deferred component holds nested `mochi:hydrate*` children (`hasIslandsOrServerIslands` is true, so `injectIslandPropsBlock` runs), and `ServerIsland.ts:187` splices that HTML into the live document inside the `<mochi-server-island>` element. `resolveIslandProps` scopes only the inside-out direction via `closest('mochi-server-island')`; a page island gets `null` there and falls through to `document.getElementById`, which per spec returns the first element in *tree order*. Since `injectIslandPropsBlock` places a block immediately before the first island referencing it (L89), a page shaped `<Widget mochi:defer/>` … `<Chart mochi:hydrate:visible data={…}/>` puts the page's `mochi-props-0` block *after* the `<mochi-server-island>`, so once the fragment lands its `mochi-props-0` wins the document-wide lookup. Timing is satisfied deterministically for `:visible` islands: `connectedCallback` hands `_doHydrate` to an IntersectionObserver (HydratableIsland.ts:38-43) and `resolveIslandProps` runs inside it (L78), so a below-the-fold island resolves long after an above-the-fold defer fetch completed. The window is actually wider than the finding states — `serverIslandClientJs` is emitted as an inline classic script while the hydration bootstrap is a deferred `type="module"` (Mochi.ts:324/367), so the defer fetch starts during parsing while even eager page islands upgrade only after parsing, giving the same collision on a slow bootstrap. Commit ea1c97bd fixed exactly the mirror-image case and asserted 'page islands … unaffected', and its test fixture only passes because it places the page block before the server island (resolveIslandProps.test.ts:22-32) — reverse the order and the same code returns the fragment payload. Result is a silent wrong-props hydration (foreign keys parse fine via devalue) or a hydration throw into the boundary; HIGH_BUG is appropriate for silent data corruption, and the fix should namespace the emit id rather than patch the lookup again.

The mechanism is described accurately — `mochi-props-N` is fully predictable, `document.getElementById` returns the first match in tree order, and `_doHydrateInner` feeds that text straight to `devalueParse` then `hydrate()` — but the finding is entirely parasitic on an HTML-injection foothold that does not exist in this codebase and whose presence would already grant more than this gives. I enumerated every `{@html}` site in the repo: all are framework-internal highlighted code, prerendered sources, or the HN demo, and that one path goes through `hn-sanitize.ts`, which allows only `p/a/i/b/code/pre` and strips *every* attribute except a URL-validated `a[href]` — no `id`, no `div`, no `script`. The DOMPurify argument is about a library this repo does not use. More importantly, the escalation claim doesn't hold: the framework ships no Content-Security-Policy (the only CSP in the tree is `packages/support/src/embedHeaders.ts`, frame-ancestors for the newsletter iframe), so any injection foothold in a Mochi app is already script execution, and even under a `script-src 'self'`-style policy the same foothold lets an attacker inject a complete `<mochi-hydratable-island component-name=… component-url=… props=…>` element — HydratableIsland falls back to the raw `props` attribute when no `props-ref` is present (HydratableIsland.ts:80) — which is a strictly more powerful primitive than shadowing an existing island's props block. The framework side is otherwise hardened: `renderIslandPropsScript` escapes every `<` to `\u003C`, and attributes go through `escapeHtmlAttr`. So there is no concrete attack against the code as shipped; this is hardening advice. It is worth noting it overlaps heavily with F1 (same lines, same global-addressing root cause), and F1's fix — per-render namespacing or sibling-scoped resolution — would incidentally remove this surface too, which is the strongest argument for doing it there.

The code is as described: `encryptPayloadBytes` deflates before sealing, `compress` defaults to `true` for payloads ≥ 80 bytes (payloadCrypto.ts:65-70), and AES-SIV in CTR mode adds no padding, so the base64url token length is an exact function of the deflated plaintext length — a byte-granular compressibility oracle. Determinism compounds it: `aessiv(key, aad)` with no nonce means identical plaintexts always yield identical tokens, so there is no per-render length jitter to hide behind. The primitive is public (`index.ts:156`) and `packages/docs/140-utility-helpers.md:79` recommends it for 'short-lived signed values such as form challenges or magic links', i.e. payloads a caller is told to treat as secrets, with no warning that mixing a secret with attacker-influenced data in one compression context is unsafe. Internally the exposed instance is server-island props: `encryptProps` passes `compress: options.compressServerIslandProps ?? true` (serverIslandCrypto.ts:31) and the resulting token is published in the page HTML as `signed-props`, while props bags naturally mix request-derived values (the docs' own `<Visitor mochi:defer name={visitorName}>`, live in `packages/site/src/demos/your-first-mochi-app/Hello.svelte:17`) with server-side data. That is precisely the BREACH setup, and the classic attack applies: drive the victim's browser to render pages with adaptive guesses in the controlled prop and read response length off the wire. I checked the other call sites and none are vulnerable on their own — the image payload is src+transform params with no secret (imageCrypto.ts:15), and captcha/clearance plaintexts are entirely server-generated — so reachability depends on an app's prop composition rather than on framework-internal data. I keep MEDIUM: the weakness class is real and acknowledged industry-wide, the fix (default `compress: false`, opt in per call site, or pad to buckets) is cheap, but practical exploitation needs a length observer and a secret/attacker-data mixed payload, so this is a defaults-and-documentation defect rather than a live hole in the shipped sites.

The factual core is right — `Bun.inflateSync(payload)` at payloadCrypto.ts:96 is called with no output ceiling, and `decryptPayload` then materialises a second copy as a UTF-8 string (L81) — but the amplification premise does not hold for anything the framework seals, and the authentication gate is stronger than the finding allows. Only a token the server itself minted under the live `MOCHI_KEY` and the matching AAD survives the SIV tag check, so the attacker cannot author a bomb; they can only replay one the app produced. I enumerated every mint site: image requests pack src+transform params bounded by URL length (imageCodec/imageCrypto.ts:15), captcha tokens are `{iat, nonce, bits}`, clearance tokens are `{iat, bits}`, and server-island props are whatever the app passes. So reaching a 1000:1 payload requires an app that funnels multi-megabyte attacker input into island props — and in that app the original page route already performs the strictly more expensive half of the work (devalue stringify *plus* deflate of the same megabytes) on every render, and page routes are the ones that actually carry rate limiting (`checkRouteLimit` is wired at Mochi.ts:981/1211 for page and api only). The attacker therefore gains no meaningful amplification over simply hammering the route that produced the token, and no framework-owned path can produce an oversized token at all. The suggested cap (declared length in the authenticated flags region, or a `payload:maxInflatedBytes` filter) is reasonable defence-in-depth — the island endpoint being both unauthenticated and unrate-limited makes a bound cheap insurance — but as shipped there is no exploitable decompression bomb, matching the finder's own 'low' confidence.

Every step of this one checks out against the source. `encryptProps` writes the devalue-parsed *plaintext* of the props it just sealed into `ctx.debugBarData.serverProps[token]` (serverIslandCrypto.ts:35-42), keyed by the exact token the client holds. `renderComponent` shallow-copies that bag onto `RenderResult.debugBarData` (ComponentRegistry.ts:1801-1802), the page handler spreads it into `debugInfo` (Mochi.ts:951), and `createShellRenderer` emits `<script>window.__mochi_debug=${jsonForHtml(opts.debugInfo)}</script>` into the body whenever `registry.debugBarEnabled` (Mochi.ts:356) — readable by every visitor and by any script on the page, which is a complete defeat of the confidentiality property the module header and svelteAstPreprocess.ts:297-299 both claim for these tokens. The gate is a build flag, not auth: `debugBarEnabled = development && (options.debugBar ?? true)` (Mochi.ts:503), and `ctx.debugBarData` is populated only for `page` kind under that flag (requestSetup.ts:150-159). The 'dev mode in production' claim is verified end to end, not inferred: `packages/site/src/lib/debugBarEncode.ts:1` states it outright, its base64url rewrite is explicitly cosmetic anti-crawler encoding that the client decodes losslessly, `packages/site/package.json` sets `"dev": "NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts"`, and the deployed `Dockerfile` ends with `ENTRYPOINT sh -c "exec bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}"` — so the shipped image runs with `development: true`. `types.ts:478-483` documents keeping the debug bar with `liveReload: false` for 'production-like deployments', making this a supported configuration rather than an accident. The corroborating detail is also accurate: `appendDebugTail` puts `ctx.cookies.peekAll()` — every request cookie, `HttpOnly` included — into the same page-readable global (Mochi.ts:192-194), and the comment at Mochi.ts:179-181 confirms the static `__mochi_debug` fields are baked into the *cached* body, so with page caching one visitor's decrypted props can be served to another. The deployed site's own island props are demo data, which is why I keep MEDIUM rather than raising it, but the framework-level disclosure is real and the recommendation (don't record plaintext into a bag that is serialized into the page) is the right fix.

Confirmed by reading the endpoint end to end. `decryptProps` checks only the SIV tag and the component-name AAD (serverIslandCrypto.ts:47-49); there is no `iat`, TTL, session binding, or nonce in the sealed envelope, and AES-SIV's determinism means a given props bag yields the same token for the life of `MOCHI_KEY`. The endpoint is genuinely unauthenticated: `KIND_POLICY.island` sets `csrf: false` (requestSetup.ts:67), the handler at Mochi.ts:1559-1696 performs no identity check — it decrypts, strips `islandId`/`__mochi_ah`, compiles and renders — and unlike page and api routes it never calls `checkRouteLimit`, so the token is the sole authorization for that render and it is replayable without limit. The token travels as `?props=` in the URL (ServerIsland.ts:142-150), the canonical place reverse proxies, CDNs and load balancers log by default. The contrast the finding draws is real and I verified both halves: `captcha.ts:50` seals `{iat, nonce, bits}` and `verifyCaptcha` enforces an age window, and `clearance.ts:13`/`hasValidClearance` seal `iat` and bound it with drift tolerance — the props path alone omits this. The docs actively teach the risky shape (`<UserAvatar mochi:defer userId={123} />`, 'use it for personalized fragments') and warn only that `mochi:defer mochi:hydrate` makes props client-visible, never that props are not an authorization boundary and that tokens never expire. Mitigating facts keep this at MEDIUM rather than higher: the island render executes with the *replayer's* request context, so a replay does not impersonate a session, and whoever held the page already held the token — the incremental harm is the unlimited lifetime for a leaked token (access logs, cached pages, shared HARs) plus the absence of any revocation short of rotating `MOCHI_KEY`, which mochiConfig.ts also notes invalidates every image URL. That is a textbook missing-expiry finding on a bearer capability, and sealing `iat` with a configurable window is the proportionate fix.

The structural observation is accurate — `ssrInstance ??= new DeferReloadState(name)` is a module-level singleton shared by every concurrent SSR render and created from whichever name arrived first — but neither stated consequence materialises, because of the constructor's own early return. `DeferReloadState`'s constructor returns at L16-18 when `typeof window === 'undefined'`, *before* `this.reloading = isReloadingDeferredIsland(name)` and before any subscription, so the instance carries exactly the field-initializer defaults (`false`, `0`, `null`, `null`) for its whole life. A hypothetical per-name SSR instance would carry those same defaults, because the island registry is empty by construction server-side — `registerDeferredIsland` is only ever called from `ServerIsland.connectedCallback` in the browser (deferInvalidation.ts:20-28, ServerIsland.ts:24/35) — so `isReloadingDeferredIsland(name)` is unconditionally `false` during SSR. The claim that 'per-name server-side reads are silently wrong' is therefore false in effect: sharing one object is observationally identical to per-name objects, and the only difference, reference identity, is not something user code can meaningfully depend on. I checked the real consumers: `packages/site/src/demos/defer-invalidation/Controls.svelte` and `ErrorModes.svelte` take four different names and only ever read `.reloading`, `.count`, `.lastReloadOk`, `.lastReloaded`, which the docs table describes as reporting fields; nothing in the framework writes to them either. The residual hazard the finding names — a public API object with writable fields pinned for the process lifetime, so an app that assigned to one would leak across requests — is genuine hardening value (freeze it, or return a throwaway per SSR call since nothing retains it), but it requires app code to write to documented read-only state, and no code path in the framework or this repo produces incorrect output today.

Verified in both files. `DeferReloadState`'s constructor calls `subscribeDeferredIsland(name, cb)` and drops the returned unsubscriber (deferReloadState.svelte.ts:20), and `subscribeDeferredIsland` genuinely returns a working `off()` that nobody ever calls (deferInvalidation.ts:40-43). The instance cache is pinned with `pinGlobal`, which is a plain strong reference on `globalThis` with no eviction and no weak semantics (utils/globalState.ts:5-9), so each distinct name permanently retains one state object plus one registered mitt handler for the page's lifetime. The teardown path that does exist is for a different registry: `unregisterDeferredIsland` removes the element from `__mochi_deferred_islands__` and deletes the name key when empty (deferInvalidation.ts:49-59), but it never touches `__mochi_defer_reload_states__` or the listener emitter — so after a `<mochi-server-island>` unmounts, its state object and listener survive. Growth is driven by legitimate, documented usage rather than misuse: the docs tell users to name islands, and per-row reloadable islands (`deferReloadState(`row-${id}`)`) or a name derived from a client-side filter/search key each add a permanent entry, which for a long-lived page with virtualised or infinitely-scrolled rows accumulates without bound. The L37 comment is honest that per-read instances would leak worse, but memoising by name trades a per-read leak for an unbounded per-name one rather than removing it. Practical impact is modest — a small object and a closure per distinct name, reset by any full navigation — so BUG is the right severity, and keying the cache off the island element, or tearing down on last unregister, is the fix.

Confirmed: `warned` is a module-level `Set<string>` with no cap and no pruning (inlineServerIslands.ts:7-15), and both key shapes embed caller data — `invalid:${String(opts.name)}` (L26) and `inline:${opts.name}` (L31). The function is hot by construction: the preprocessor emits `{#if __mochi_inline_island__(…)}` at every non-visible `mochi:defer` call site (svelteAstPreprocess.ts:344, imported as `shouldInlineIsland` via the `mochi-server-island-runtime` virtual module), so it executes on every render of such a site, in page renders as well as island-endpoint renders. Both warning branches sit ahead of the budget check and so fire in either context. Growth needs an app to pass a dynamic `name`, which the reload API explicitly invites, plus one of the two warned-about mistakes: a non-string name (`name: item.id` yields `invalid:1`, `invalid:2`, … — note `isReloadableIslandName` requires a non-empty string, deferInvalidation.ts:16-18) or `inline: true` on a named island, which is ignored but otherwise harmless so a developer may well ship it. In either case each distinct id permanently adds a string to a process-lifetime Set — and emits a `logger.warn` line per distinct value, so the log spam is arguably the louder symptom — and an attacker who drives the id space (paginating or searching a large table) amplifies it at will. The dedup intent at L9 is correct; only the key space is wrong, and the `inline:` message does not even depend on the name, so a per-component flag or a bounded LRU fixes it. Impact is bounded by the misuse precondition and by string size, so BUG with low practical severity is the right call.

The arithmetic is correct and I verified the surrounding wiring: `!(st.budget > 0)` admits `Infinity`, `st.budget--` leaves `Infinity` unchanged, the budget is armed only at the island endpoint from `applyFilter('serverIsland:inlineBudget', DEFAULT_INLINE_BUDGET, …)` (Mochi.ts:1604), and it is indeed the sole termination condition for nested inlining — grepping `islandInline` shows no separate depth counter anywhere. But this is not a defect the framework can be charged with, because the only way to reach it is for an application to deliberately return an unbounded budget from a `number`-typed filter, and the resulting unbounded nesting is exactly what that value asks for. The `!(> 0)` style exists to fail closed on *garbage* (`NaN`) from a misbehaving filter; `Infinity` from a numeric filter is a deliberate 'no limit', not garbage, and a large finite value (`1e9`) would hang identically — so `Infinity` is not a special-case gap in the guard, it is the general consequence of letting the app choose the bound. Reaching a hang additionally needs a self- or mutually-recursive deferred island (A rendering `<A mochi:defer/>`, or A↔B), which is an unusual structure that is already infinite in principle; the default budget of 32 is what makes it terminate. Nothing in the repo registers this filter, and `inlineNestedIslands` defaults on with the 32 budget, so there is no reachable failure as shipped. Normalising the filter result to a finite non-negative integer is still sensible input hygiene and I would not argue against it, but as a vulnerability or bug it requires the app to request the behaviour it then suffers — consistent with the finder's own 'low' confidence and 'not reachable on defaults' note.
